title: Car won't go into gear
h1: Why won't my car go into gear or move?
metaDesc: Car won't go into gear or won't move in Drive? A few questions show if it's the shifter, fluid, clutch or an axle, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: car wont move in drive or reverse
put it in drive and nothing happens
engine revs but car won't move
stick shift won't go into gear
car won't move when I press the gas
shifter moves but car doesn't move
grinding when trying to get into gear
intro: When a car won't go into gear, the big clues are whether the shifter moves, whether the engine revs without the car moving, and whether you have an automatic or a manual. Some causes are simple, like a shift lock or a parking brake left on. Others, like a transmission that has lost its fluid, mean the car shouldn't be driven. Answer a few questions to find out which.
safety: Before getting out, set the parking brake firmly. If the shifter or transmission is faulty, the car may not really be in Park.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, turn the engine off and step away.
Don't keep revving the engine to force it to move. That can turn a repairable problem into a ruined transmission or clutch.

q_type.q: Is your car an automatic or a manual (stick shift)?
q_type.help: If there are only two pedals, gas and brake, it's an automatic. A manual has a third pedal, the clutch.

opts.a: Automatic (two pedals)
Manual (three pedals, with a clutch)
I'm not sure

q_auto.q: What happens when you try to put it in Drive or Reverse?
q_auto.help: Keep your foot firmly on the brake while you shift.

opts.a: The shifter won't move out of Park at all
The shifter moves, but the car doesn't move and the engine just revs when I press the gas
It goes into gear, but only after a pause of a few seconds, often with a thump
It moves in Reverse but not Drive, or the other way round
It goes into gear, but the car feels held back, like the brakes are on
I'm not sure

q_auto_display.q: When you move the shifter, does the gear letter on the dash (P, R, N, D) change to match?
q_auto_display.help: Most cars show the selected gear on the instrument panel or next to the shifter.

opts.a: No, it stays on the same letter or doesn't match the shifter
The shifter feels loose or floppy
Yes, it matches, but the car still won't move
I'm not sure
There's a reddish puddle under the car, or it was leaking fluid recently
I heard a bang or loud clunk, then it stopped moving
It had been slipping or revving oddly between gears before it quit
None of these / I'm not sure

q_manual.q: What happens when you try to drive off?
q_manual.help: The clutch is the pedal on the far left. Pressing it to the floor lets you change gears.

opts.a: The clutch pedal feels soft, sinks to the floor, or stays down
The clutch pedal feels normal, but gears grind or won't go in, especially from a stop
The gear goes in, but when I let the clutch out the engine revs and the car barely moves
I heard a bang or loud clunk, and now it won't move in any gear
The shifter feels loose or floppy and doesn't select gears
I'm not sure

result.title: The shift lock may be holding the shifter in Park
result.now: With the key in ON or the engine running, press the brake pedal firmly and try again. If it still won't move, use the shift lock release, a small slot or button near the shifter (your owner's manual shows where).
if: If the brake lights don't come on when you press the pedal, a brake light switch or fuse is the likely cause. Get that fixed before driving in traffic, because drivers behind you can't see you stop.
If the car is parked on a slope, set the parking brake, hold the brake pedal down and shift with a firm, steady pull. The car's weight can bind the Park lock.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks or is much harder to press than usual, don't drive the car. Have the brakes checked first.
If the release lets you shift but the problem keeps coming back, have it checked soon rather than relying on the release.
result.why: Automatic cars won't let you leave Park unless they sense your foot on the brake. If that signal doesn't arrive, a small lock keeps the shifter in place. The cause is often simple and electrical rather than a transmission failure, but a shop can confirm it with a quick test.

causes.name: Faulty brake light switch or blown fuse
causes.clues: The brake lights don't come on when you press the pedal.
causes.against: If the brake lights work normally, look at the other causes first.

causes.name: Weak or dead battery
causes.clues: Dim dash lights, slow cranking, or a push-button or dial shifter.

causes.name: Car's weight resting on the Park lock
causes.clues: Parked on a slope without the parking brake set first, and the shifter feels jammed rather than locked.

causes.name: Failed shift lock part or shift cable
causes.clues: The brake lights work, and the manual release lets you shift.

you: Have someone check whether the brake lights come on.
Check the brake light fuse.
Try the shift lock release.

result.title: A delay before it engages often points to low fluid or internal transmission wear
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days. If your car has a transmission dipstick, check the fluid level the way your owner's manual describes first.
if: If the delay gets longer, or the engine revs before the car moves, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see reddish fluid under the car, don't drive it until the leak is found.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke from under the car, turn the engine off and step away.
If it slips or loses drive while you're moving, pull over when it is safe and have it towed.
result.why: An automatic transmission uses fluid pressure to engage each gear. When the fluid is low or worn, or internal seals are tired, it can take longer to build that pressure. A shop will usually check the fluid and codes before deciding on any repair, and catching it early often means a smaller one.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid
causes.clues: Reddish spots where you park, or the delay is worse when the engine is cold.

causes.name: Old or burnt fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid with a burnt smell, or no transmission service in many years.

causes.name: Worn internal seals or valve body problem
causes.clues: Harsh or late shifts as well as the delay.

causes.name: Transmission control fault
causes.clues: A check engine or transmission warning light is on.

you: Look for reddish spots where you park.
Note whether it's worse when cold or after a long drive.
Check the fluid if your car has a dipstick.
shop: Transmission fluid level and condition check

result.title: The transmission may have lost one or more of its gears
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a transmission shop or a general repair shop.
if: If it's blocking traffic, put it in Neutral and push it out of the way with help, or call roadside assistance.
If you find the fluid very low, tell the shop. A leak may be a much easier fix than internal damage.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Drive and Reverse use different clutches or bands inside the transmission. When one direction works and the other doesn't, one of those may have failed or isn't getting enough fluid pressure. A car that can't be relied on to go forward isn't safe in traffic, and forcing it can cause more damage.

causes.name: Low transmission fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or delayed engagement in the weeks before.

causes.name: Worn or failed clutch pack or band inside the transmission
causes.clues: That gear slipped or flared before it quit.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or valve body fault
causes.clues: A transmission or check engine light, or the car seems stuck in one gear.

you: Look for reddish fluid under the car.
Note any warning lights on the dash.

result.title: The parking brake or a stuck brake may be holding the car back
result.now: Make sure the parking brake is fully released (pedal, lever or electronic switch), then try moving off gently. If the car still feels held back, don't keep driving it. Have the brakes checked first.
if: If a wheel smokes, smells burning or is too hot to go near, stop. Let it cool and have the car towed.
If it still feels held back with the parking brake off, have the brakes checked before driving any further.
If the brake pedal feels hard, soft or different than usual, or the red brake warning light stays on, have it checked before driving.
result.why: If you can feel the transmission go into gear but the car struggles to roll, something is resisting the wheels. A parking brake that's on, partly on or frozen, or a brake caliper that won't release, are common causes. A brake that stays on can overheat, so it shouldn't be driven on.

causes.name: Parking brake still on or partly on
causes.clues: The brake warning light is on, or the electronic parking brake didn't release.

causes.name: Parking brake frozen or rusted
causes.clues: Cold, wet weather, or the car sat unused for a while.

causes.name: Stuck brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others, there's a burning smell, or the car pulls to one side.

you: Check the parking brake warning light.
After a short, slow move, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to feel for one that's much hotter.
shop: Parking brake cable and mechanism check

result.title: The shifter may have come disconnected from the transmission
result.now: Set the parking brake firmly and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you can't be sure the car is in Park (or in gear, on a manual), block the wheels as well as setting the parking brake.
If the shifter suddenly goes loose while you're driving, pull over safely and stop as soon as you can.
result.why: A cable or rod connects the shifter to the transmission. If it breaks, or the small bushing that holds it falls apart, moving the shifter no longer changes gears, so the transmission can be left in any gear, including one that lets the car roll. It's often a small part, but the car isn't safe to use until it's checked and fixed.

causes.name: Worn-out shift cable bushing
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose or floppy. This is a common wear part.

causes.name: Broken, stretched or disconnected shift cable or linkage
causes.clues: The dash gear display doesn't match the shifter position.

causes.name: Linkage not reconnected after a repair
causes.clues: Recent work near the transmission or under the center console.

you: Note whether the dash gear display changes when you move the shifter.
Note whether the shifter feels loose or moves with almost no resistance.

result.title: The transmission may have lost its fluid
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed so the leak can be found and fixed before more damage is done.
if: If you can see where it's leaking, take a photo for the shop.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: An automatic transmission needs fluid pressure to engage any gear. A large leak, like a split cooler line or a damaged pan, can drain it quickly, and the car stops moving. Running it with too little fluid, even briefly, can ruin the transmission. A shop will find the leak and check for damage before refilling and road-testing.

causes.name: Leaking transmission cooler line
causes.clues: A puddle toward the front of the car and a sudden loss of drive.

causes.name: Leaking pan, gasket, seal or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips under the middle of the car, or a recent fluid service.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Fluid on the inside of a front wheel or tire.

you: Note the color of the fluid and where the puddle is.
Check the dipstick if your car has one.
shop: Check for damage from running low

result.title: An axle or drive shaft may be broken
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed, ideally on a flatbed truck.
if: If the engine sounds normal and you can feel it go into gear, but the wheels don't turn, that points more to a broken axle or drive shaft than to the transmission.
If fluid is pouring out under the car, tell the tow driver and the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: A loud bang or clunk followed by no movement often means something between the transmission and the wheels has snapped. The engine and transmission may be fine, but the power isn't reaching the wheels. Clicking when turning in the days before often points to a worn CV joint. A shop will inspect the axles, drive shaft and differential to confirm.

causes.name: Broken CV axle
causes.clues: Clicking when turning beforehand, a front-wheel-drive car, or grease spattered inside a front wheel.

causes.name: Broken drive shaft or U-joint
causes.clues: A rear-wheel or all-wheel-drive vehicle, with clunking or vibration beforehand.

causes.name: Broken parts inside the differential or transmission
causes.clues: Grinding noises, or a fluid leak after the bang.

you: Look behind each front wheel for a torn rubber boot or sprayed grease.
From beside the car, without getting under it, look for a drive shaft hanging down.

result.title: The transmission doesn't seem to be sending power to the wheels
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop and ask for a transmission diagnosis.
if: If the fluid turns out to be very low, a leak may be the real cause, which is often a smaller repair.
If a transmission or check engine light is on, the stored codes will help the shop.
If you smell burning fluid or see smoke, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: When the gear display shows Drive and the engine revs but the car doesn't move, the transmission isn't engaging. Possible reasons include very low fluid, worn internal clutches, a failed torque converter or pump, or an electronic fault. A shop will usually check the fluid, codes and pressure before deciding what has failed. Revving it harder won't help and can cause more damage.

causes.name: Very low transmission fluid
causes.clues: Reddish spots where you park, or delayed engagement in the weeks before.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches
causes.clues: Slipping, or the revs flaring between gears before it quit.

causes.name: Failed torque converter or transmission pump
causes.clues: A whine that rises and falls with engine speed.

causes.name: Electronic control fault
causes.clues: A transmission warning light, or it was stuck in one gear before it quit.

you: Check the fluid if your car has a dipstick.
Note any warning lights on the dash.

result.title: The clutch hydraulics may have failed
result.now: Don't drive it. Check the clutch fluid reservoir and look for leaks, then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic to the car.
if: If the reservoir is low and there's fluid near the clutch pedal or under the car, a leaking clutch master or slave cylinder is a possible cause.
If the brake pedal also feels soft, don't move the car at all. On many cars the brakes and clutch share one fluid reservoir.
If the reservoir is low, don't just top it up and drive. Not seeing a leak doesn't rule one out, and on a shared reservoir the brakes can be affected too.
result.why: Most manual cars use fluid pressure to release the clutch. If the pedal sinks or stays down, that pressure may be gone, so the clutch can't release and gears grind or won't go in. Forcing it into gear risks damaging the transmission and leaves you without control of when the car moves.

causes.name: Leaking clutch slave cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid dripping near where the engine meets the transmission.

causes.name: Failed clutch master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid on the carpet or under the dash near the pedal, or the pedal sinks slowly.

causes.name: Air in the clutch line
causes.clues: Recent clutch work, or the reservoir ran low.

causes.name: Broken clutch cable
causes.clues: An older or cable-operated car, and the pedal went limp with no resistance.

you: Check the clutch fluid reservoir level (your owner's manual shows where).
Look for wet fluid near the pedal and under the car.
shop: Clutch master and slave cylinder test

result.title: The clutch may not be fully releasing
result.now: Press the clutch all the way to the floor and wait two or three seconds before selecting first or Reverse, and book a clutch check in the next few days.
if: If the gears go in easily with the engine off but grind with it running, that points to the clutch not releasing. Tell the shop.
If the clutch pedal starts to feel soft or sinks, or the brake pedal feels soft, stop driving and have it towed.
If you smell burning from the clutch, stop and let it cool before trying again.
If it only grinds going into Reverse, make sure the car is fully stopped and pause a moment first. Many manuals grind in Reverse if you shift too quickly.
result.why: Gears go in smoothly only when the clutch fully disconnects the engine from the transmission. If it doesn't fully release, parts inside are still spinning and the gears clash. Low fluid, air in the line or a worn clutch are common reasons, and a shop will usually check the hydraulics before looking at the clutch itself.

causes.name: Low clutch fluid or air in the line
causes.clues: The pedal feels slightly soft, or the clutch only releases right at the floor.

causes.name: Worn or warped clutch parts
causes.clues: The clutch grabs very high or very low, or shudders when you pull away.

causes.name: Worn synchros in the transmission
causes.clues: It grinds mainly in one gear, especially when shifting quickly while moving.
causes.against: If it grinds going into every gear from a stop, the clutch is more likely.

you: Check the clutch fluid reservoir.
With the engine off, try selecting gears. If they go in easily, the clutch is the more likely problem.

result.title: The clutch may be slipping badly
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed to a shop.
if: If you smell burning, let the car sit and cool before anyone works on it.
If the car doesn't creep at all when you let the clutch out, a broken axle or drive shaft is also possible. Tell the shop.
result.why: When the gear goes in but the engine revs without moving the car, the clutch may no longer be gripping. That usually builds gradually as the clutch wears, then suddenly gets much worse. Oil on the clutch, or a hydraulic problem keeping it partly released, can do the same, so a shop will check those before replacing the clutch.

causes.name: Worn-out clutch disc
causes.clues: Revs flaring in higher gears for a while before, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Clutch hydraulics not letting it fully engage
causes.clues: The pedal is slow to come back up, or feels different than usual.

causes.name: Oil leaking onto the clutch
causes.clues: Oil dripping from where the engine meets the transmission.

causes.name: Broken axle or drive shaft
causes.clues: A bang beforehand, and no movement at all in any gear.
causes.against: If the car creeps slightly as you let the clutch out, the clutch is more likely.

you: Note whether you smell burning after trying to move.
Look for oil dripping between the engine and transmission.

result.title: A shop needs to see what's stopping it from moving
result.now: Set the parking brake, note what you see and hear when you try to shift, and have it towed or call roadside assistance.
if: If you see a puddle under the car or smell burning, don't try again. Tell the tow driver.
If the shifter won't leave Park, check whether the brake lights work. That's a common, simple cause.
If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't try to move the car. Tell the tow driver and the shop.
result.why: Without knowing whether the shifter moves, whether the engine revs, or whether there's a leak, it's hard to narrow it down safely. A technician can quickly tell a shifter problem from a fluid, clutch or axle problem.

causes.name: Shifter or shift lock problem
causes.clues: The shifter won't move, or feels loose.

causes.name: Low fluid or a transmission fault
causes.clues: A reddish puddle, or the engine revs but the car doesn't move.

causes.name: Clutch or axle problem
causes.clues: A manual car, or a bang or clunk before it stopped moving.

you: Record a short video with sound of what happens when you try to shift. It helps the shop a lot.
